newsitem.title: UK: Axa-UAP deal worries European insurers.
newsitem.headline: Axa-UAP deal worries European insurers.

text.p: By Gordon Mackenzie, Insurance Editor
European insurers began reviewing their strategic positions on Tuesday after France's AXA announced plans to absorb rival UAP and form a new super insurance group.

The move, which ousts German insurer Allianz from the top of the European insurance league, had been dreaded by European insurance industry players -- although several on Tuesday said it was inevitable.
Merger rumours concerning UAP have been kicking around the insurance market since the beginning of the year, when its low share price made it vulnerable.

Market sources say several U.S. insurers considered launching a bid for UAP but dropped the idea because it would be difficult to undertake such a move on a group of political importance in France. UAP was formerly owned by the French state, and was only privatised in 1994.

Axa was the name that came up time and again as a candidate for a strategic alliance, a merger, or a takeover bid. However right up until last Friday executives continually denied that their companies were in talks.

Although UAP is by far the bigger of the two, Axa is clearly the driving force in the new operation. It is this fact, coupled with the announcement that Axa chairman Claude Bebear will head up the combined group, that is giving rival insurers food for thought.
Axa is regarded by analysts and competitors alike as the quality player in the French insurance sector -- in fact many see it as one of the highest quality and best managed insurers in Europe.
It is much more diversified than its domestic rivals. Its largest business sector is the U.S. through the 60.5 percent ownership of the Equitable Cos Inc acquired last year.

Axa also gained access to Asian and Far East markets through its 51 per cent stake in National Mutual, Australia's second largest life insurer which in turn controls Hong King's second largest life insurer, National Mutual Asia.
Axa has made it clear it plans to use these for expansion into Asia and China.

Neither does AXA have the same bank and property loan problems faced by UAP, AGF and GAN. These three were tempted by optimistic earnings projections for property investment in the late 1980's which left them painfully over-stretched when the property boom ended in the early 1990s.
Axa has seen steady increases in earnings of around 20 per cent in the last two years, and it surprised the market in September with a massive 52 per cent leap in first half profits.

Bebear said on Wednesday he wants the new group to achieve cost savings of 500 million francs in 1998, and that the new group will not only be number one in France, but that it would hold leading positions in the key markets of UK, Belgium, Germany and Spain. In addition the alliance will offer critical mass in the Netherlands and Italy, as well as the continued opportunities provided by Axa's positions in north America and Asia.

One market insurance industry source said: "Every European insurer with an interest in any of these markets will be rushing to the planning room to see how they are affected. Many will be very worried."

However the new group will have its problems. The French insurance market is notoriously difficult, although some analysts believe French composite insurers' earnings will improve after the meltdown of 1994 and 1995.

Insurance premiums were raised by up to 10 percent in January 1995 and by a smaller amount at the beginning of 1996. So far losses have been relatively light with the exception of the Credit Lyonnais headquarters fire in May.

UAP owns the Colonia subsidiary in Germany, and AXA last year launched a direct selling operation there which expects to register 40,0000 new customers this year and aims to be Germany's biggest car insurer by the year 2000. On September it announced the formation of a similar operation in Spain.
However German non-life insurance profits are expected to decline as the full force of the competition unleashed by recent deregulation takes effect.
"This deal certainly makes the combined group big, " said a leading insurance analyst, "but it remains to be seen whether big will be beautiful."
